1:
All of them link this psalm to the one before it, and two notice the same hinge. C.H. Spurgeon observes that the last psalm ended with a blessing, the word there rendered happy being the very word here rendered blessed, so that the two songs are joined by a catch-word and share a close community of subject. Keil and Delitzsch make the same observation into a structural argument: this psalm follows that one for the same reason that the second psalm follows the first, since in both pairs one begins with the word blessed and one ends with it; and the two supplement each other as the parables of the treasure in the field and of the one pearl do, for what makes a man happy appears in the earlier psalm as a gift coming as a blessing and here as a reward coming as a blessing, the single word for reward there being here expanded and unfolded. John Calvin calls this psalm a kind of appendage to the other. Adam Clarke makes it the second part of the same poem and supplies a scene: the man who was said there to have a numerous offspring is here seen sitting at table with his large family, while a visitor coming in pronounces him happy.

Whether the psalm’s maxim can be believed is the question John Calvin raises and C.H. Spurgeon answers. Calvin says the maxim that those who fear God are blessed, and blessed especially in the present life, is so much at variance with the common opinion of men that very few will assent to it; the adage that it is best not to be born at all, or to die as soon as possible, has long since been received by the common consent of almost all men. Spurgeon meets that adage head on: some think this life an evil, an infliction, a thing upon which rests a curse, but it is not so, and it is not true that it would be to the God-fearing man something better not to be. Matthew Henry states the same in the older formula, that godliness has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. Augustine of Hippo takes a third way, arguing from a martyr who had none of these domestic blessings and yet has them perfectly in the Body of him who is described here,.

The test of the fear itself is pressed by two of them. John Calvin notes that the second half of the first verse adds a mark by which the servants of God are distinguished from those who despise him, since the most depraved boast of fearing God, so that the prophet requires the attestation of the life; the fear of God and the keeping of his law are inseparable, and the root must necessarily produce its fruit. C.H. Spurgeon analyses the fear itself into reverence, dread to offend, anxiety to please, and entire submission. On the promise of eating the labour of one’s hands, Adam Clarke insists that nobody is exempted from labour, only that the hand of violence shall not be permitted to take away the produce. Matthew Henry counts a double promise, that a man shall have something to do, since an idle life is a miserable and uncomfortable one, and that others shall not eat the bread out of his mouth. Charles Ellicott makes the emphasis exact, since the position of the particle gives, for it is the labour of thine hands thou shalt eat; and he observes that this picture of a successful and peaceful husbandry throws a whole flood of light on the condition of the land and of a people now not nomadic but agricultural. John Gill adds the spiritual sense, of men who labour in prayer and in attendance on the word.
3:
Whether the figure is a vine on a wall or a wife in a house is disputed. John Gill takes the horticulture seriously: the vine is a weak and tender tree needing to be propped, and is often fastened to the sides of a house; and a Jewish commentator observes that it is the only tree men plant within doors, trained out through a hole or window to have the sun and air, so that its root is within and its branches without — whence the modest woman is within the house while her children, like the branches, go out to work. Adam Clarke denies the whole basis of that: being about the house sides is spoken of the wife and not of the vine, just as being round the table is spoken of the children and not of the olive plants, and it does not appear that vines were planted against the walls of houses there, nor olive trees kept in pots or tubs indoors as they are in parts of Europe. Charles Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by another route: the inner part of the house is no doubt meant, the women’s quarter or the sides of the inner court, and this is no more out of keeping with the figure of the vine than the table is with that of the olive plants, since a strict custom allotted a more private part of the dwelling to the women even before the later habit of secluding them. He adds that we are to think of the good housewife engaged within at her household duties, and not of the idle gossip who sits at the door of her house on a seat in the high places of the city; and he notes that the comparison of children to the healthy young shoots of a tree is common to all poetry, being latent in a phrase like the scion of a noble house.

How the last two verses are to be construed divides the readers three ways. Charles Ellicott holds that the optative is plainly required, so that the sense is may the Lord bless thee and mayst thou see; and of the closing clause he says the conjunction spoils the passage, since the psalm concludes with the prayer, peace upon Israel. Adam Clarke agrees at least for that last clause, which he would render as a wish that peace be upon Israel and that God favour his own cause. Keil and Delitzsch take a third construction, that the promissory future is followed by imperatives which call upon the God-fearing man to do at once what the promises have already made certain for him; and they add that every blessing the individual enjoys comes from the God who has taken up his abode in the holy city and is perfected in a share of that city’s prosperity and the whole church’s. John Gill keeps the verbs as promises and takes the blessing out of the sanctuary of the word and ordinances and the divine presence in them. Adam Clarke reads the same verse practically, that in every approach to God in his house the man shall have an especial blessing and shall see the cause of God flourish in his lifetime, and the verse before it as a bargain, a great price for a small consideration, since he who fears God shall have as much domestic good as may be useful to him. Charles Ellicott notes that the poet first calls attention to the charming picture of domestic bliss he has drawn and then points his moral, and illustrates the children’s children from a Latin poet on seeing the sons of one’s sons and those who shall be born of them. John Wesley says only of the olive plants that they are numerous, growing and flourishing.
